editorial.headline: IoT by Commission: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Custom IoT systems work is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks a foreigner from registering the activity there.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity concerns commissioned, integrated IoT-system solutions rather than products made for general sale. The work combines consulting, design and creation of a bespoke system requested by a client, using modifications to existing hardware—such as sensors and microcontrollers—and/or to the embedded software within that IoT hardware. The intervention may sit in the physical device, its embedded software, or both. What matters is the made-to-order modification and integration of existing components.

The boundary is equally important. This classification does not cover chip manufacture, IoT software publishing, IoT software development, the manufacture of transmission equipment or connectivity modules, or the manufacture of final IoT-based products. It instead defines a professional-services lane: working with existing hardware and its embedded software to assemble a tailored integrated solution. The wording asks the reader to look at the nature of the work, not simply at the presence of IoT technology. Registration is available at every stated business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—placing the activity across the full stated scale range.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%, meaning the national framework permits the foreign stake to reach that full ceiling. A foreign investor may therefore hold up to 100% of the activity under the national PMA position. This national openness is clear, but it belongs to the national framework alone; it is not a conclusion about a particular provincial registration process.

Bali changes the answer completely for PMA registration. The Bali status is Blocked (risk class): a foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk across every scope is Low/Medium-Low, and it is therefore caught by the Bali moratorium. That island-wide, permanent provincial rule blocks PMA registration for activities in the Low and Medium-Low risk bands. The record places the block in May 2026. The decisive Bali factor is the risk classification at the Besar scale, not a reduction in the national shareholding ceiling. National openness and Bali registration are two different layers of the record; a 100% national ceiling does not displace a Bali PMA-registration block.
